summary: Defines two mechanisms for a client in a conference to learn whether the conference focus supports CCMP, using, for example, the Call-Info header, so the client can use centralized conferencing operations. This helps conferencing clients make use of the extra features.

plainLanguage.summary: A way for you in a meeting to learn the host supports the special remote controls.

subtitle: Discovering CCMP support in conference servers

tldr.problem: SIP clients that support the Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol need to know if a conference focus also supports it, but no discovery mechanism exists.
tldr.mechanism: Two mechanisms allow clients to discover CCMP support: a Call-Info header with a ccmp purpose parameter, or a service URI with ccmp purpose in the conference event package.
tldr.outcome: SIP clients can now determine if a conference focus supports advanced CCMP operations without trying multiple approaches.

facts.label: Two discovery methods
facts.value: Call-Info header and service URI purpose

facts.label: Required consistency
facts.value: Both methods report the same information

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: INVITE, OPTIONS, and event package notifications

today: RFC 7082 is informational and remains active, defining mechanisms that enhance SIP conferencing interoperability.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content:
Centralized Conferencing is a framework where participants exchange media through a central server. The Centralized Conferencing Manipulation Protocol (CCMP) lets clients manage conferences directly: adding participants, changing their roles, controlling media streams. RFC 6503 defines CCMP.

The problem: a SIP client can discover that a conference control server supports CCMP, but not whether a conference focus (the endpoint in charge of a specific conference) supports it. Without this knowledge, clients cannot use advanced CCMP features.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you join a meeting and want to use special controls to manage participants. First you need to know if the meeting host has those controls available.

sections.title: The Two Discovery Methods
sections.content:
The RFC describes two mechanisms. The first uses the Call-Info header, which is sent in SIP requests and responses. It carries a URI (the XCON-URI of the conference focus) and a purpose parameter with the value ccmp. This signals that the focus supports CCMP without requiring the client to parse the URI format.

The second mechanism defines a new purpose value in the SIP conferencing event package. A client that subscribes to the conference event package can examine the <service-uris> element and look for a URI with <purpose>ccmp</purpose>.

The Call-Info method suits clients that do not use the event package, such as back-to-back user agents. The service-uri method suits clients that already subscribe to conference event notifications.
sections.plainLanguage: Method one puts a flag in a message saying the conference host supports CCMP. Method two puts the flag in a subscription notification about the conference details.

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content:
A UA that subscribes to the conference event package examines the event data to see if a service URI with purpose ccmp is present. A UA that does not subscribe can send an OPTIONS request to the conference server and check the Call-Info header in the response.

Servers MUST provide consistent information through both channels: if a server indicates CCMP support through the Call-Info header in OPTIONS responses, it must also indicate support through the conference event package. This ensures clients never need to try both methods.
sections.plainLanguage: If you are watching for messages about the conference, look for the ccmp marker. If not, ask the server with an OPTIONS message.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: This RFC does not introduce new security threats. CCMP already allows clients to discover if a conference server supports CCMP using DNS mechanisms. The solution reuses existing headers and data elements without creating new attack surfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: These discovery methods are safe and do not create new security problems for networks.
